Out of Seat. Again. And Again. And Again.
Every single morning you pack his bag, walk him to school, and by 9:15 there's already a message on the app: "He was under his desk during carpet time." You know he's not doing it on purpose. You've watched him sit down with absolute determination — jaw set, hands flat on the desk — and within 90 seconds his body has found some other position entirely. He's not misbehaving. His body just won't cooperate.

Sitting Still Isn't Passive — For a Child With Sensory Differences, It's the Hardest Athletic Event of Their Day
The Neuroscience: Three Systems Govern Seated Stability
🧠 Vestibular System (inner ear → cerebellum → postural muscles): Detects movement, gravity, and balance. In sensory-seeking children, this system is underresponsive — it needs MORE input than sitting still provides, driving the body to rock, tip, and move.
🧠 Proprioceptive System (muscles/joints → somatosensory cortex): Tells the brain where the body is in space. Poor proprioceptive processing means the child doesn't clearly feel their sitting position, causing constant micro-adjustments.
🧠 Postural Control Network (core muscles → basal ganglia → motor cortex): Maintains upright position automatically in most children. In children with low muscle tone, DCD, or sensory processing differences, this requires conscious effort — depleting cognitive resources needed for learning.
In Plain English
For most children, sitting upright is automatic — like breathing. Their nervous system handles it without them thinking about it.
For your child, sitting upright is a manual task. Every minute of sitting requires active physical effort. While their classmates use 100% of their cognitive energy for learning, your child is spending 60–80% of it just staying in the chair.
This is not willful misbehavior. This is a neurological reality.
The body will seek the input it needs. If sitting doesn't provide enough vestibular or proprioceptive input, the nervous system will generate that input through rocking, tipping, standing up, or leaving the seat entirely. The 9 materials in this guide work by providing that input through the chair itself.
Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience (2020): DOI: 10.3389/fnint.2020.556660 | Sensory Integration Theory (Ayres) | NCAEP Evidence-Based Practices (2020)
Your Child Is Here — And There Is a Clear Path Forward
The WHO Care for Child Development package establishes that postural control is a prerequisite skill for academic participation. The school entry age (5–6) is ahead of neurological readiness for many children — particularly those with any developmental difference.
Age 3–4
Sits for 5–10 min structured play. Core control emerging.
Age 5–6 — School Starts Here
Expected to sit 15–20 min for classroom tasks. Many children with ASD/ADHD/DCD/hypotonia are not neurologically here yet.
Age 6–8 — H-705 Intervention Window
Vestibular & proprioceptive systems continue maturing. With seating supports, functional seated attention becomes achievable.
Age 7–9 — Mastery
With intervention + seating supports → measurable improvement in on-task behavior and academic output.
Age 8–12 — Independence
Self-regulation strategies including independent movement management established.

The "Your Child Is Here" Reframe: The 5–6 year classroom expectation was designed for a statistically average child. Your child may be neurologically 12–18 months behind on postural control — not as a deficit, but as a developmental timeline. Sitting difficulties commonly co-occur with: Autism Spectrum Disorder · ADHD · Developmental Coordination Disorder · Hypotonia · Sensory Processing Disorder · Anxiety Disorders. The Technique: Sensory-Based Seating Modification & Postural Support Protocol
Parent-Friendly Alias: "The Right Seat for Your Child's Body"
A structured set of 9 clinically validated therapy materials that modify the standard classroom chair environment to meet a child's specific sensory-motor needs — providing vestibular input, proprioceptive feedback, postural support, and structured movement opportunity so the child can remain seated and access learning without expending all cognitive energy on the act of sitting itself.
🎯 Domain
School Readiness + Motor Development + Sensory Regulation
👶 Age Range
4–12 years
⏱️ Frequency
Daily, during all seated academic activities. Ongoing use — not time-limited.

This Technique Exists at the Intersection of Four Therapy Disciplines
Because the child's sitting challenge doesn't care about professional silos. Every discipline brings a different lens — and together they form a complete clinical picture.
Occupational Therapist (Primary Lead)
Conducts postural and sensory profile assessment. Selects, trials, and calibrates seating supports. Trains parents and teachers in implementation. Monitors and adjusts based on outcomes.
Uses: Wobble cushion, wedge, foot rest, compression vest, weighted lap pad
ABA Therapist / BCBA
Implements structured movement break schedules using behavioral principles. Designs token reinforcement for successful seated intervals. Measures in-seat duration data to track progress.
Uses: Visual timer, movement break cards, fidget management protocols
Special Educator
Coordinates seating accommodations within IEP/504 framework. Trains classroom teachers. Ensures seating supports are available and correctly used. Advocates for appropriate consequences.
Uses: All 9 materials in the classroom environment
Neuro-Developmental Pediatrician
Rules out medical causes. Determines whether ADHD medication warrants consideration. Signs off on clinical seating support recommendation for school.
Uses: Comprehensive assessment → clinical recommendation letter

Material 1: Wobble Cushion / Wiggle Seat
Dynamic Seating
Sensory Input
Material 1 of 9
What It Does
Provides vestibular + proprioceptive input while the child remains seated. Activates core muscles through mild instability — giving the nervous system the movement input it seeks, without requiring the child to leave the seat.
Price Range: ₹500–1,500
✅ Pinnacle Recommends: Textured surface, 33–38cm diameter, latex-free, with pump
Best For
  • Sensory-seeking children with high movement drive
  • Children who rock, tip chairs, or constantly shift position
  • Vestibular underresponsive profiles
Pro Tip
Inflate more (less wobble) for first sessions. Deflate slowly as the child adapts and builds tolerance to the instability input.
Search: Wobble Cushion 33cm sensory →
Material 2: Chair Resistance Bands (Bouncy Bands)
Proprioceptive Input
Lower Body Regulation
Material 2 of 9
What It Does
Stretches across the front legs of a standard chair; gives feet a place to push, kick, and bounce — meeting lower-body proprioceptive needs without the child ever leaving the seat. One of the simplest, highest-impact materials in the entire kit.
Price Range: ₹200–600
✅ Pinnacle Recommends: Latex-free, medium resistance, fits standard chair legs
Best For
  • Children who kick, tap, or swing feet constantly
  • Lower-body proprioceptive seeking behavior
  • Pairs beautifully with wobble cushion for dual-input approach
DIY Alternative
Bicycle inner tube (free from cycle shop) or thick rubber band. Same resistance mechanism; feet push against elastic — identical therapeutic action at zero cost.
Search: Bouncy Bands Chair Classroom →
Material 3: Weighted Lap Pad
Deep Pressure
Proprioceptive
Material 3 of 9
What It Does
Provides grounding deep pressure to the thighs; calms and organizes the nervous system; creates clear body-in-space awareness. Often described by children as "my heavy blanket" — a calming, anchoring sensation that reduces the need for active movement seeking.
Price Range: ₹800–2,500
✅ Pinnacle Recommends: ~10% of child's body weight; soft washable cover; 25×40cm
Best For
  • Children who feel "unanchored" in their seat
  • Anxious restlessness and sensory seeking overlap profiles
  • Proprioceptive processing difficulties
Safety Note
Do not exceed 10% of the child's body weight. Never use on children with respiratory difficulties or hypotonia grade III+ without physician clearance.
Search: Weighted Lap Pad Child Therapy →
Material 4: Foot Rest / Foot Positioning Support
Postural Support
Ergonomic Foundation
Material 4 of 9
What It Does
Provides base-of-support for children whose feet don't reach the floor. Achieves the critical 90-90-90 ergonomic position (ankles/knees/hips at 90°). Eliminates the root cause of up to 40% of out-of-seat behavior — because dangling feet make stable upright sitting physically impossible.
Price Range: ₹300–1,500
✅ Pinnacle Recommends: Height-adjustable, non-slip base, 20–30cm width
The 90-90-90 Test
Sit the child. Check: ✅ Ankles at 90° ✅ Knees at 90° ✅ Hips at 90° ✅ Feet flat on surface. If any angle fails, this is the first support to implement — before any other material.
DIY Alternative
Thick hardcover book stack; wooden crate; shoebox filled with sand. Provides identical ground-contact stability at zero cost.
Search: Adjustable Foot Rest Children →
Material 5: Therapy Ball Chair / Ball Seat
Dynamic Active Seating
Core Engagement
Material 5 of 9
What It Does
A stability ball with a base ring for classroom use. Engages core muscles continuously; allows micro-movement in all directions while maintaining a seated position. Higher sensory input than a wobble cushion — best for children with strong sensory-seeking drives and adequate core strength.
Price Range: ₹1,500–4,000
✅ Pinnacle Recommends: 45cm ball for ages 6–9; base ring is essential; assess with OT first
Important Safety Notes
  • Base ring is non-negotiable — never a ball alone on a standard chair
  • Do NOT use for children with core weakness (use wedge + foot rest instead)
  • Do NOT use for anxiety-driven restlessness — instability can increase anxiety
  • OT assessment required before introducing this material
Search: Therapy Ball Chair Base Ring →
Material 6 & 7: Compression Vest + Seat Wedge Cushion
Deep Pressure
Trunk Input
Postural Support
Materials 6 & 7 of 9
Material 6: Compression Vest
Provides full-trunk deep pressure, calming the nervous system and improving body awareness. Particularly effective for children who feel "unanchored" in their seats. Snug but not restrictive — 20–30 min use periods. Washable fabric essential.
Price Range: ₹1,000–3,500
Safety: Never during physical activity. Never on a child who cannot communicate discomfort without adult monitoring.
Search: Compression Vest Child →
Material 7: Seat Wedge Cushion (Slant Cushion)
A 10-degree anterior pelvic tilt makes neutral spine the default position. Reduces slouching fatigue and the energy cost of upright sitting. Best for core weakness rather than sensory seeking — it stabilizes rather than activates.
Price Range: ₹600–1,500
✅ Pinnacle Recommends: 10° angle, non-slip base, dense foam, washable cover
Search: Seat Wedge Cushion Posture →

Hand Regulation
Attention Regulation

Material 8: Quiet Classroom Fidgets
Silent hand-based sensory tools that satisfy the proprioceptive input drive in the hands — preventing hand restlessness from escalating to whole-body movement disruption.

Safety First: Read This Before Placing Any Material Under, On, or Around Your Child's Seat
🔴 RED — DO NOT PROCEED
  • Child has undiagnosed vestibular disorder or balance impairment → Get OT clearance first
  • Weighted items on children with respiratory difficulties or hypotonia grade III+ → Physician clearance required
  • Ball chair on a child highly anxious about instability → OT assessment first
  • Any seating support on a child who cannot independently remove it → Adult immediate supervision only
  • Compression vest on a child who cannot communicate discomfort → Adult monitoring at all times
🟡 AMBER — MODIFY & MONITOR
  • Child has latex allergy → Use latex-free products only (verify before purchase)
  • Wobble cushion: inflate more (less wobble) for first sessions; deflate slowly
  • Weighted lap pad: do not exceed 10% of child's body weight
  • Compression vest: maximum 20–30 min periods; never during physical activity
  • Ball chair: must have base ring; never a ball alone
🟢 GREEN — PROCEED WHEN
  • Child is regulated (not in meltdown or highly distressed)
  • Child has eaten and is not in acute hunger
  • Child is medically well (no fever, acute ear infection)
  • Environment is set up correctly (see Card 18)
  • All materials checked for damage, proper inflation, correct sizing

🛑 STOP IMMEDIATELY IF: Child shows increasing distress · Attempts to remove support in a way suggesting discomfort · Complains of pain or pressure · Becomes MORE dysregulated · Ball chair rocks beyond controlled movement. Questions about safety: 9100 181 181 (Free, 24×7, 16+ languages). Indian J Pediatr RCT (2019): DOI:10.1007/s12098-018-2747-4
Set Up Your Space — The Environment Is the First Intervention
Get this right and 40% of session success is already guaranteed. The physical environment either supports or undermines everything that follows.
Remove From Space
  • ❌ Excess toys and objects not needed for the activity
  • ❌ Screens (unless screen-based task)
  • ❌ Other children if possible for initial sessions
  • ❌ Food/snacks that might distract
Environment Settings
  • 💡Lighting: Natural or warm; avoid harsh fluorescent if sensitive
  • 🔊Sound: Low background; no TV; white noise may help
  • 🌡️Temperature: Comfortable; compression vest can cause overheating
  • 📍Chair position: Against wall or in corner reduces 360° distraction

90-90-90 Test: Sit child. Check: ✅ Ankles at 90° ✅ Knees at 90° ✅ Hips at 90° ✅ Feet flat on foot rest or floor. If any angle fails, adjust chair height or foot rest height before beginning any session. Sensory Integration Theory (Ayres) + PMC10955541
Is Your Child Ready? The Readiness Check
60 seconds of assessment now prevents 45 minutes of frustration later. This check is not optional — it is the clinical gating event that determines whether to proceed, modify, or postpone.
☐ Fed and not hungry
Hunger amplifies sensory reactivity. A hungry child cannot regulate.
☐ Rested
Post-nap or morning sessions outperform post-long-day sessions significantly.
☐ Calm or slightly alert baseline
Not mid-meltdown; not severely distressed.
☐ No acute illness
Fever, ear pain, or illness shifts the entire sensory threshold.
☐ No major dysregulation in last 30 min
System needs reset time after a significant event.
☐ Positively associated with the space
If the study nook is associated with previous failures, introduce supports in a new location first.
☐ Support materials already positioned
Do not try to place wobble cushion after child is seated and resistant.
✅ 5–7 Met → GO
Proceed to Step 1: The Invitation
⚠️ 3–4 Met → MODIFY
Shorter session, fewer materials, lower demand
🔴 0–2 Met → POSTPONE
10 min preferred calming activity; reassess. A postponed session is a wise clinical decision.
Step 1 of 6
⏱️ 30–60 seconds
Step 1: The Invitation
Every session begins with an invitation, not a command. The child is brought into the activity through playful, low-demand engagement. The wobble cushion, resistance band, and foot rest are already in place — you're inviting the child to discover them, not comply with them.
"Hey, I set up something cool on your chair. Want to check it out before we start?"
Never: "Go sit down." Never: "It's time for sitting practice." Both create immediate resistance.
What Acceptance Looks Like
  • Child moves toward the chair
  • Child touches or examines the wobble cushion
  • Child asks "what is this?"
  • Child sits voluntarily (even briefly)
What Resistance Looks Like & How to Respond
  • Child ignores/walks away → Don't pursue; try again in 5 min with more playful framing
  • Child removes wobble cushion → Let them; introduce one support at a time
  • Child says "I don't want to" → "That's okay. Want to just try it for one second?"
ABA Pairing Procedures | OT Just-Right Challenge principle
Step 2 of 6
⏱️ 1–3 minutes
Step 2: The Engagement
The child is seated. Now the therapeutic materials begin doing their work. Do not narrate them clinically — let the child's body discover the input naturally.
✅ Engagement
Spontaneous movement on wobble cushion; feet pushing on band; settles into task
⚠️ Tolerance
Accepts materials without movement; compliant but not naturally integrating
🔴 Avoidance
Removes material; moves off seat; requests to stop → reduce demand, go slower
"You are working so hard right now. I can see you're really focused. That's exactly it." — Deliver this when child remains seated and engaged for 2+ minutes. Immediate. Specific. Warm.
PMC11506176 — Structured material introduction in sensory integration sessions
Step 3 of 6
⏱️ 5–15 minutes — Core Therapeutic Window
Step 3: The Therapeutic Action
The Active Ingredient: The child is completing an actual task (reading, writing, worksheet, puzzle) while the seating supports provide continuous background sensory input. The therapeutic event is not the sitting itself — it is the simultaneous task completion + sensory regulation happening together.
Wobble Cushion
Child should have subtle micro-movement (shifting, gentle rocking). This is CORRECT. Do not redirect this movement unless the child risks falling off. The movement IS the therapy.
Resistance Band
Feet pushing against band rhythmically = sensory seeking being met productively. Feet completely still = band not being used (prompt gently: "remember your feet can push on that").
Weighted Lap Pad
Should remain on child's lap throughout task. If it slides off and child doesn't replace it, this material may not be providing noticeable benefit for this child's profile.
Foot Rest
Child's feet should be fully flat on the surface at all times. If feet are partially on or dangling, adjust foot rest height immediately.
Visual Timer
Running during the seated task. Child can see time remaining. When timer ends → proceed to movement break card.

Child Response Spectrum:✅ Ideal: Subtle movement on cushion + feet active on band + eyes on task. ✅ Acceptable: Seated, engaged, using some supports. ⚠️ Concerning: Increasing agitation, attempts to leave, crying. PMC10955541 — Core action 40–60% of session time; maximum 40-min sessions for effectiveness.
Step 4 of 6
⏱️ 3–5 minutes additional rounds
Step 4: Repeat & Vary
"3 good sessions > 10 forced sessions." A child who completes three 5-minute seated tasks with genuine engagement has received more therapeutic benefit than a child forced through 30 minutes of resistive sitting.
Vary the Task
Switch from writing to reading to a puzzle. Seating supports remain constant; only the task changes. This builds generalization: the supports work across activities, not just one.
Vary the Support Combination
Day 1: Wobble + Resistance Band. Day 2: Wedge + Foot Rest + Lap Pad. Compare child's engagement to confirm which combination matches the profile.
Vary the Timer Duration
Week 1: 5 min timer. Week 2: 7 min. Week 3: 10 min. Build stamina incrementally using the same mechanism — gradual dosage increase.
Vary the Movement Break
Rotate through break card options (chair push-ups / wall push-ups / stretches / jumping jacks) to prevent habituation to any single break activity.
Satiation Indicators (when the child has had enough): Increased movement beyond normal micro-movement · Head down on desk · Attempts to leave without completing movement break protocol · Verbal protest escalating. SI dosage research: 2–3×/week for 8–12 weeks standard.
Step 5 of 6
Step 5: Reinforce & Celebrate — The Timing Matters More Than the Words
The Neuroscience of Reinforcement: Reinforcement delivered within 3 seconds of desired behavior creates the neural association that drives repetition. Reinforcement delivered 10 seconds later does not form the same connection.
"You just sat through that entire timer. Your whole body did it. I'm so proud of you — that was REAL work."
Not: "Good job." Not: "Good sitting." Not: "You were so good today." — These are generic and don't reinforce the specific achievement of the child.
Social Praise
The specific script above; add physical celebration if child welcomes it (high five, hug).
Token Economy
Star chart or sticker chart specific to seated work sessions. Visual, cumulative, motivating.
Choice Reinforcement
"You earned 5 minutes of free choice because you nailed that timer." Natural, meaningful consequence.
Milestone Tangibles
Small preferred item for milestone achievements: first 10-minute seated session, first completed week of all timers.
ABA Reinforcement Principles + BACB ethical guidelines | Token economy systematic reviews for autism intervention
Step 6 of 6
⏱️ 2–3 minutes
Step 6: The Cool-Down — No Session Ends Abruptly
The cool-down is as therapeutic as the session itself. An abrupt ending breaks the positive association that makes the next session possible.
The Transition Warning Script
"Two more minutes, then we're going to wrap up and take a break."
When timer ends: "Timer's done! Amazing work. Now we do our cool-down before we put everything away."
If the Child Resists Ending
This is a positive sign — they were engaged. Don't extend the session.
"I know you want to keep going. That's great! We can do more tomorrow. For now, cool-down then break."
NCAEP Evidence-Based Practices (2020): Visual supports and transition support are evidence-based practices for autism spectrum disorder.
Capture the Data: 60 Seconds Now Saves Hours of Guessing Next Month
Data collection is not bureaucratic overhead. It is the clinical mechanism that tells you what's working, what to change, and when your child has made real progress.

What If It Didn't Go As Planned? Session Abandonment Is Not Failure — It's Data
Every difficult session tells you something clinically useful. Here is what your data means and exactly what to do next.
Problem 1: Child Refused the Wobble Cushion Entirely
Why: Novelty aversion; sensory aversion to texture or instability; previous negative associations.
Fix: Introduce the wobble cushion away from the chair first — on the floor during TV time. Normalize it before expecting classroom use. Try smooth side vs. textured side.
Problem 2: Child Became MORE Hyperactive on Wobble Cushion
Why: The wobble cushion is an ALERTING tool for some nervous systems. Over-aroused children may dysregulate further with vestibular input.
Fix: Switch to the WEDGE CUSHION (stabilizing, not activating). Or use wobble cushion only after heavy work activity that has calmed the system first.
Problem 3: Child Kept Removing the Weighted Lap Pad
Why: Weight too heavy; fabric uncomfortable; child is a proprioceptive avoider, not seeker.
Fix: Reduce weight by 30%. Try different fabric. If still removing it, switch to compression vest instead.
Problem 4: Child Still Got Out of Seat Despite All Supports
Why: Task demand exceeded current capacity; child may need shorter intervals; support combination doesn't match specific sensory profile.
Fix: Reduce seated task duration by 50%. Increase movement break frequency (every 3 min instead of 5). Consult OT to re-profile.
Problem 5: Teacher Refused to Allow Supports at School
Why: Lack of awareness; classroom management concerns; school policy gaps.
Fix: Request OT + teacher meeting with research evidence (PMC11506176). Request IEP or 504 meeting if formally diagnosed. Pinnacle provides school consultation.
Problem 6: Child Became Severely Distressed During Session
Why: Sensory overload; support felt restraining; wrong day or wrong state.
Fix: STOP. Remove all supports immediately. Provide preferred calming activity. Do NOT retry for 24 hours. Call Pinnacle helpline before next session.
Problem 7: Supports Worked at Home But Child Refuses at School
Why: Environmental generalization is a separate skill; peer awareness and social anxiety about "looking different."
Fix: Have OT speak to the class about "tools that help everyone focus differently." Consider under-clothing options (compression shirt) that are invisible to peers.
ABA functional analysis principles + Pinnacle center clinical problem-solving protocols
Adapt & Personalize — No Two Children Sit the Same Way
The protocol is a framework, not a prescription. Here is how to tune this approach to YOUR child's specific neurological profile.
Ages 4–6
1 support only; 3–5 min sessions; heavily reinforced from the first second.
Ages 7–9
2–3 supports; 8–12 min sessions; involve child in choosing their own tools.
Ages 10–12
Full kit; 15–20 min; teach child to self-manage and advocate for their needs at school.

Good Day / Bad Day Protocol: Good day: Full kit, full duration, harder task. Medium day: 2 supports, moderate timer, easier task. Rough day: 1 support only, 3-min timer, pure preferred activity — just maintain positive association. Individualized intervention planning across OT/ABA/SLP clinical practice guidelines

They announce themselves quietly, in the form of your child staying in their chair for one more minute than they did on Monday."

Week 3–4
Week 3–4: The Child Begins to Anticipate — That's the Neural Pathway Forming
40%
Consolidation Phase
Behavioral changes signal that supports are being integrated into the child's regulatory system.
✅ Consolidation Indicators
  • Child places wobble cushion on chair themselves before sitting (without prompting)
  • Child pushes feet against resistance band habitually (automatic, not conscious)
  • Seated duration increases measurably — check your tracking sheet
  • Child requests "my heavy blanket" (weighted lap pad) independently
  • Reduced protest when visual timer starts
  • First signs of school generalization: teacher notes fewer out-of-seat incidents
🧠 What This Means Neurologically
The child's nervous system is learning: when I use these tools, my body feels organized, and organized feels better than dysregulated. This is Pavlovian regulation — and it's working.
When to Increase Intensity
If child is using all 3 primary supports comfortably AND seated duration has increased by 30%+ → add the 4th support, or increase timer duration by 2 minutes.
"You may notice you're more confident too. Your anxiety about the school notes is decreasing. You have a protocol now. That's not nothing — that's everything."
🏆 Progress Arc
Week 5–8
Week 5–8: Mastery Indicators
75%
Mastery Phase
All three mastery criteria must be met before considering support reduction.
✅ Duration Mastery
Child consistently maintains seated position for full timer period (15+ minutes with supports) across 4+ consecutive sessions.
✅ Generalization
Seated behavior improves in at least ONE setting beyond the primary intervention setting (e.g., homework at grandparents', school desk, restaurant).
✅ Maintenance
Seated duration does not drop significantly on days when 1 support is accidentally omitted — the gains are holding independently.
Generalization Plan: Week 6: School desk (with teacher support) → Week 7: Restaurant or religious service setting → Week 8: Grandparents' home. One new setting per week.
PMC10955541: measurable outcomes across 24 studies | BACB mastery criteria standards

Red Flags: When to Pause and Seek Professional Consultation
Trust your instincts. These signs indicate that the current approach needs professional reassessment — not more persistence.
🚨 Seated Duration DECREASING Over 3+ Weeks
Despite consistent use of supports → The support combination is not matched to the child's profile. OT re-assessment is needed immediately.
🚨 New Behavioral Escalation at School
Not present before interventions began → Possible activating/calming mismatch; possible unrelated medical or psychiatric issue emerging.
🚨 Skin Irritation or Physical Discomfort
From compression or weighted items → Discontinue immediately; seek dermatological and OT review before resuming.
🚨 Child's Distress INCREASES Over Time
The technique or pace is wrong for this child. Formal sensory profile evaluation is required before continuing.
🚨 Motor Coordination Appears to Be Worsening
Rule out neurological cause immediately. Immediate pediatric neurology referral required — do not delay.

Frequently Asked Questions
Every question a parent has asked at a Pinnacle center. Answered here first — so you never have to wait to move forward.
❓ My child's school won't allow a wobble cushion because it's "disruptive." What can I do?
Request an OT assessment that generates a formal clinical recommendation letter. Schools in India are legally required to provide reasonable accommodations for children with developmental diagnoses (RTE Act + RPWD Act 2016). A letter from a registered OT changes the conversation from "can we?" to "how do we?" Pinnacle's school consultation service assists with this. Call 9100 181 181.
❓ My daughter doesn't have autism or ADHD. She just can't sit still. Do these supports apply?
Yes. Sitting difficulty is not diagnosis-specific. Many children without any formal diagnosis have sensory processing differences, low muscle tone, vestibular processing variation, or developmentally appropriate movement drives that are not matched to classroom expectations. The supports in H-705 address the underlying mechanism (sensory-motor), not the diagnostic label.
❓ Won't my child become dependent on the wobble cushion forever?
Two answers. First: "dependent" on glasses doesn't mean glasses are harmful — it means the glasses match the need. Second: the seating supports, when combined with OT intervention building underlying postural and sensory processing skills, are progressively withdrawn as the child's capacity develops. The goal is independence; the supports are the bridge.
❓ Which support should I try first?
Match to your child's primary challenge: Sensory seeker (constant movement) → Wobble cushion first. Feet don't reach the floor → Foot rest first. Collapses/slouches → Wedge cushion first. If you don't know: Wobble cushion is the most universally useful first-trial support. Call 9100 181 181 for a free telephone OT guidance session.
❓ How long will my child need these supports?
Varies by underlying cause. Children with sensory processing differences may use supports through childhood with gradual reduction. Children whose challenge is primarily developmental lag often need supports for 1–2 years. Children with permanent neurological differences may need lifetime supports — just as glasses are a lifetime support. OT assessment gives your child's specific prognosis.
❓ Can I use more than one support at the same time?
Yes — the most effective protocols combine 2–4 supports simultaneously. Most evidence-supported combination: Wobble cushion OR Wedge cushion (seating base) + Foot rest (stability base) + Resistance band (lower body input) + 1 fidget (hand regulation). Add weighted lap pad or compression vest based on sensory profile.
❓ Supports work at school but homework at home is still a battle. Why?
Environmental generalization. The supports work where they've been consistently established. Replicate the exact same support combination at the homework space: same cushion, same foot rest, same timer, same movement break protocol. Consistency is the active ingredient — the environment must match.
